## Acknowledgments

**Unto the Honorable, Prudent, and Wise Magistrates of the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg, and to all curious Christian Readers, grace and peace.**

Herein is completed the noble and wondrous Book of the magnificent Venetian, Messer Marco Polo, which declareth the great marvels of the East, of Cathay, and of the mighty Khan of the Tartars.

First and foremost, let boundless thanks be rendered unto Almighty God, who in these latter days hath bestowed upon mankind the ingenious and subtle art of impressing letters by metal without the stroke of a quill, whereby such profitable knowledge might be multiplied and spread among the principalities of the earth.

I must humbly acknowledge the labor of the learned Master Heinrich, who took it upon himself to turn this history from the Latin tongue into our own plain German, that the burghers and merchants of this city might read of the spices and silks of the Orient without the barrier of a scholar’s language.

Likewise, my gratitude is bound to the worshipful Herr Sebaldus of the Merchant Guild, whose generous purse did furnish the stout rag paper and the fine lamp-black ink required to bring this heavy labor to the press. Without his patronage, these marvels of India and Persia would have remained locked within the dusty scriptoriums of the monasteries.

Finally, I commend the diligent journeymen of my workshop, who stood long hours at the press to strike these pages clean and true.

## Who is this Book for?

**The Enterprising Merchant:** If your trade involves the acquisition of pepper, ginger, silk, or precious stones, this book serves as a practical geographical manual. You will find detailed accounts of the major trading hubs from Hormuz to Cathay, including the preferred currencies (such as the Great Khan’s paper money), safe routes, and the relative dangers of bandits and deserts along the Silk Road.

**The Sovereign and the Statesman:** For kings, princes, and dukes who wish to understand the geopolitical architecture of the world beyond the Levant. This text offers a comprehensive operational overview of the Mongol Empire under Kublai Khan, detailing his military structure, courier system, administrative laws, and the unfathomable scale of his revenues.

**The Cartographer and Cosmographer:** If you are tasked with updating the *mappae mundi* (world maps), this document will radically expand your borders. It provides definitive proof of navigable seas to the east of Asia, island nations such as Cipangu (Japan), and detailed distances measured in days of travel.

**The Theologian and the Friar:** For those tracking the spread of Christendom or seeking alliances against the Saracens. You will find intelligence on the locations of Nestorian Christians, the religious tolerance of the Tartars, and the various idolaters that populate the Indies.

## An Epistle to the Reader, from the Printer

To the curious and patient reader, greetings.

Before you embark upon the text that follows, it is proper that you are given some instruction on how to receive it. We have labored at great length to strike these pages from metal type, bringing the words of the Venetian, Messer Marco Polo, into our plain German tongue. But the architecture of these Eastern realms is exceedingly complex, and to comprehend such vast and foreign territories without guidance places a heavy burden upon the mind.

You will find no familiar landmarks here. The author speaks of kingdoms that dwarf our own Holy Roman Empire, of cities crisscrossed by bridges of marble, of stones that burn like wood, and of paper that commands the value of gold.

It is natural for the mind to rebel against such claims, to assume them to be the fictions of a romancer. Yet I urge you to approach this topography with a clear and open judgment. Marco Polo was not a poet, but a merchant and an administrator in the court of the Great Khan. His accounts are laid out not for idle entertainment, but as a systematic record of provinces, revenues, and trade routes.

Therefore, do not attempt to swallow this book whole. Read it measure by measure. Allow the structure of his journey—from the deserts of Persia to the high plains of the Tartars, and onward to the coastlines of the Indies—to build a new map within your thoughts.

We have placed this volume before you so that the boundaries of your world might be expanded. Bear the weight of its strangeness, and your understanding shall be greatly enriched.

God preserve you in your reading.

*— F.C., Nuremberg.*

# **Book I**: Account of Regions Visited or Heard of on the Journey from the Lesser Armenia to the Court of the Great Kaan

This is loose matter that is immediately under Part 1 (Book I: Account of Regions Visited or Heard of on the Journey from the Lesser Armenia to the Court of the Great Kaan), but is not under any Chapter.

## Chapter 1: Here the Book Begins; and First it Speaks of the Lesser Hermenia.

[wuE3pTmy3-.jpeg.enc](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/firescript-577a2.appspot.com/o/imgs%2Fapp%2FSCFH%2FwuE3pTmy3-.jpeg.enc?alt=media&token=69b53a2b-6b16-42b6-a787-300b58e404d8)

There are two Hermenias, the Greater and the Less. The Lesser Hermenia is governed by a certain King, who maintains a just rule in his dominions, but is himself subject to the Tartar. The country contains numerous towns and villages, and has everything in plenty; moreover, it is a great country for sport in the chase of all manner of beasts and birds.

It is, however, by no means a healthy region, but grievously the reverse. In days of old the nobles there were valiant men, and did doughty deeds of arms; but nowadays they are poor creatures, and good at nought, unless it be at boozing; they are great at that. Howbeit, they have a city upon the sea, which is called Layas, at which there is a great trade. For you must know that all the spicery, and the cloths of silk and gold, and the other valuable wares that come from the interior, are brought to that city. And the merchants of Venice and Genoa, and other countries, come thither to sell their goods, and to buy what they lack. And whatsoever persons would travel to the interior (of the East), merchants or others, they take their way by this city of Layas.

## Chapter 2: Of the Province called Turkomania, where are the Cities of Kogni, Kaisariah, and Sevasta, and of its Commerce.

[115xlSDz4L.jpeg.enc](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/firescript-577a2.appspot.com/o/imgs%2Fapp%2FSCFH%2F115xlSDz4L.jpeg.enc?alt=media&token=8ea7df26-e5be-450b-9ac4-2b9715eb8fbe)

> [!NOTE]
> **Lesser Hermenia (Cilician Armenia) vs. Turkomania (Anatolia)**
>
> When Marco Polo traveled, he didn’t view these as overlapping regions. He landed his ship at the busy port city of **Layas (Ayas)** on the coast of Lesser Hermenia. To get to Turkomania, his caravan had to travel north from the coast, climb through the treacherous mountain passes of the Taurus Mountains (such as the famous Cilician Gates), and emerge onto the high inland plateau of Turkomania to continue their journey east toward the Mongol Empire.

In Turkomania there are three classes of people. First, there are the Turkomans; these are worshippers of Mahommet, a rude people with an uncouth language of their own. They dwell among mountains and downs where they find good pasture, for their occupation is cattle-keeping. Excellent horses, known as Turquans, are reared in their country, and also very valuable mules.

The other two classes are the Armenians and the Greeks, who live mixt with the former in the towns and villages, occupying themselves with trade and handicrafts. They weave the finest and handsomest carpets in the world, and also a great quantity of fine and rich silks of cramoisy and other colours, and plenty of other stuffs.

Their chief cities are Kogni, Kaisariah, and Sevasta, of which last Saint Blaise was Bishop. They are all subject to the Great Kaan, who chooses a king to rule over them. And now we will leave this province, and speak of the Greater Hermenia.

## Chapter 3: Of the Greater Hermenia, with what it Containeth.

**A Vast Land:** He describes Greater Hermenia as an enormous country, noting that it contains many cities and villages.

Here is a list of 10 cities mentioned by Marco Polo in *The Travels*, along with their modern-day equivalents and brief context:

1.  **Layas (Ayas):** The bustling port city on the Mediterranean coast of Lesser Hermenia where the Polos began their overland journey.
2.  **Kogni (Konya):** A major inland city on the Anatolian plateau (Turkomania) noted for its urban commerce and fine carpets.
3.  **Kaisariah (Kayseri):** Another prominent trade and craftsmanship city in Turkomania.
4.  **Kinsay (Hangzhou):** Described by Polo as the most splendid and magnificent city in the world, located in eastern China.
5.  **Cambaluc (Beijing):** The grand winter capital of Kublai Khan’s vast Mongol Empire.
6.  **Ciandu / Shangtu (Xanadu):** The famous summer capital of Kublai Khan’s empire, noted for its magnificent marble palace.
7.  **Ormuz (Hormuz):** A wealthy, strategically important port city on the Persian Gulf, crucial for the maritime spice trade.
8.  **Baudas (Baghdad):** The ancient city whose siege, capture, and destruction by the Mongols Polo recounts in detail.
9.  **Samarcan (Samarkand):** A major, heavily populated trade hub along the Silk Road in Central Asia.
10. **Zaiton (Quanzhou):** A massive Chinese port city, described as one of the busiest havens in the world, from which the Polos eventually sailed on their journey back to Europe.

**Tartar Encampments:** Polo mentions that during the summer months, the region is highly favored by the Tartar (Mongol) armies because of its excellent pastures for their livestock. However, they abandon the area in the winter when heavy snows make the cold intolerable.

**Mount Ararat and Noah’s Ark:** The most famous detail in this chapter is Polo’s reference to a massive, snow-capped mountain shaped like a cube. He notes that the mountain is so huge and the snow never melts, making it impossible to climb, and explicitly identifies it as the resting place of Noah’s Ark.

## Chapter 4: Code Listing

``` python
@validate_call
def transcribe(node_tree: NodeTree) -> VertexTree:
    """Transcribe every node in *node_tree* into a :class:`~guffin.vertex_tree.VertexTree`.

    Traverses *node_tree* in pre-order DFS order.  Most nodes are transcribed
    one-to-one via :func:`transcribe_standalone_node`.  Exception: a
    :attr:`~guffin.roam.node.NodeType.NATIVE_TABLE` node and all of its
    descendants are consumed together into a single
    :class:`~guffin.vertex.TableVertex` via :func:`to_table_vertex`; those
    descendants are skipped when the DFS iterator later yields them.

    When :data:`SHOULD_NORMALIZE_HEADING_LEVELS` is ``True``, computes a
    *heading_offset* equal to ``1 − min effective heading level`` across all
    nodes in the tree, so that the shallowest heading maps to level 1; when no
    heading nodes are present, or when :data:`SHOULD_NORMALIZE_HEADING_LEVELS`
    is ``False``, *heading_offset* is 0.

    Args:
        node_tree: A validated tree of raw Roam nodes.

    Returns:
        A :class:`~guffin.vertex_tree.VertexTree` in document (DFS) order, with
        :attr:`~guffin.vertex_tree.VertexTree.ref_vertices` populated from
        :attr:`~guffin.roam.node_tree.NodeTree.refs_by_id`.  Referenced native-table
        nodes are consumed into a single :class:`~guffin.vertex.TableVertex` (with their
        row/cell descendants) just as in-tree tables are, so a cross-page table reference
        resolves to a complete table.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If any anchor node has neither a ``title`` nor a ``string`` field set.
    """
    min_level: Final[HeadingLevel | None] = (
        min_effective_heading_level(node_tree.tree_network) if SHOULD_NORMALIZE_HEADING_LEVELS else None
    )
    heading_offset: Final[int] = (1 - min_level) if min_level is not None else 0
    logger.debug("heading_offset=%d", heading_offset)
    consumed: Final[set[Id]] = set()
    vertices: Final[list[Vertex]] = []
    for node in node_tree.dfs():
        if node.id in consumed:
            continue
        # A <domain>-meta:: container and its whole subtree are folded onto the parent vertex's
        # attribute_assignments (see _resolve_attribute_assignments); consume them so they are not
        # transcribed as standalone vertices.  Checked before the attribute-block guard so a meta
        # block whose value happens to parse as an attribute is still consumed (not folded twice).
        if _is_meta_block(node):
            _consume_subtree(node, node_tree, consumed)
            continue
        # Attribute blocks are folded into their parent vertex's attribute_assignments field
        # (see _resolve_attribute_assignments), not transcribed as standalone vertices.
        if node_type(node) is NodeType.ATTRIBUTE_BLOCK:
            continue
        if node_type(node) == NodeType.NATIVE_TABLE:
            table_vertex, nodes_consumed = to_table_vertex(node, node_tree)
            consumed.update(nodes_consumed)
            vertices.append(table_vertex)
        else:
            vertices.append(transcribe_standalone_node(node, node_tree, heading_offset))
    ref_vertices: Final[list[Vertex]] = []
    ref_consumed: Final[set[Id]] = set()
    # Native tables are multi-node constructs: consume each referenced table together with its
    # row/cell descendants first, so those descendants are not also transcribed as standalone
    # ref vertices.  refs_by_id is not in DFS order, so a single-pass consumed-set guard could
    # encounter a cell before its table; a dedicated table pass avoids that.
    for ref_node in node_tree.refs_by_id.values():
        if node_type(ref_node) != NodeType.NATIVE_TABLE:
            continue
        try:
            ref_table_vertex, ref_nodes_consumed = to_table_vertex(ref_node, node_tree)
        except (NotImplementedError, ValueError) as exc:
            logger.debug("skipping ref table node uid=%r: %s", ref_node.uid, exc)
            continue
        ref_consumed.update(ref_nodes_consumed)
        ref_vertices.append(ref_table_vertex)
    for ref_node in node_tree.refs_by_id.values():
        # Native tables are consumed above; attribute blocks and meta containers are not vertices.
        if (
            ref_node.id in ref_consumed
            or node_type(ref_node) in (NodeType.NATIVE_TABLE, NodeType.ATTRIBUTE_BLOCK)
            or _is_meta_block(ref_node)
        ):
            continue
        try:
            ref_vertices.append(transcribe_standalone_node(ref_node, node_tree))
        except (NotImplementedError, ValueError) as exc:
            logger.debug("skipping ref node uid=%r: %s", ref_node.uid, exc)
    return VertexTree(tree_vertices=vertices, ref_vertices=ref_vertices)
```

## Chapter 24: How the Old Man Used to Train His Assassins.

**The Deception:** The Old Man of the Mountain maintained a beautiful, secret garden modeled after the Islamic concept of Paradise. He would gather young men from the region and secretly dose them with a powerful sleeping potion. While they were unconscious, his servants would carry the youths into this hidden valley.

**The Awakening:** When the young men awoke, they found themselves surrounded by magnificent palaces, flowing runnels of milk and wine, and beautiful women singing and dancing. Believing the stories they had been told, the young men were fully convinced they had awakened in Paradise.

**The Return to Court:** After a few days of indulging in the garden’s pleasures, the Old Man would have them drugged again and returned to his standard court. When they awoke, they were deeply disappointed to find themselves back in the mortal world.

**The Oath of the Assassin:** The Old Man would interrogate the youths before his court, and they would eagerly testify that they had seen Paradise. He would then promise them that if they assassinated his enemies, his angels would carry them straight back to the garden—whether they survived the mission or were killed in the attempt.

**The Resulting Terror:** Believing wholeheartedly in this promise, the assassins became fearless, willing to undertake any murder requested by the Old Man. Consequently, he became feared by kings and princes throughout the region.

> Go thou and slay So and So; and when thou returnest my Angels shall bear thee into Paradise. And shouldst thou die, natheless even so will I send my Angels to carry thee back into Paradise.
>
> – The Old Man
